judge.reasoning:
This is a genuinely presentation-ready report for a senior home-care site-selection decision.

Section relevance (9): Every section maps tightly to the brief. Section 1 (senior concentration) targets the core 70+/65+ demand base; Section 2 (income + six-figure households) addresses the middle-to-upper-income private-pay customer; Section 3 (disability + home ownership) is exactly the right pairing for aging-in-place clinical need; Section 4 (home value + uninsured rate) sensibly translates wealth and payment friction into service-tier strategy; Section 5 synthesizes into tiered recommendations. No filler sections. Minor gap: the brief explicitly names 'nearby hospitals' as a criterion, and no section analyzes hospital proximity/healthcare access, which is a real omission for a home-nursing agency.

Narrative quality (9): The prose is specific and consistently tied to the shown numbers (e.g., Sumter's 57.7% over-65 vs. mid-pack 34.9% six-figure share; Collier's $90,835 median). It resists generic filler and delivers actionable positioning: premium private-pay in Collier/Sarasota/St. Johns, value/insurance-oriented tiers in Citrus/Highlands, financing-forward models in Miami-Dade/Palm Beach. The distinction between 'volume but moderate affluence' (Sumter) and 'affluent but less senior' (Key West/Jacksonville) is the kind of nuance an owner can act on.

Data plausibility (8): Values are largely realistic for Florida — Sumter/The Villages at ~57% over 65 and ~86% home ownership is accurate to that community; Collier/Naples incomes and home values, Monroe/Key West's ~$787K home value and elevated uninsured rate, and St. Johns' high income/low uninsured all track with real ACS-style patterns. Disability rates 15–23% and uninsured 5–15% are plausible. Two small inconsistencies: Sarasota's population appears as 452,773 in the county bubbles but 892,239 for the North Port-Bradenton-Sarasota CBSA (correctly distinguished, but worth noting), and Indian River county is repeatedly conflated with the Sebastian-Vero Beach CBSA using identical figures (166,936 population, 34.85% over 65) — reusing a metro number as a county number is a minor accuracy slip.

Visualization appropriateness (8): Chart choices are well matched — bars for ranked categorical comparisons (senior share, six-figure share, disability, home value) and bubble charts for the genuinely multi-dimensional trade-offs (senior share vs. income vs. population vs. disability). The opportunity bubble chart uses four encoded dimensions appropriately. Deductions: the report leans heavily on repeated bubble charts and bar charts of the same top-5 counties, creating some redundancy; a distribution view (histogram/violin) of senior share or income across all 21 counties would have added value and none is used despite distribution_data being a supported type.

Tool selection relevance (9): The agent picked the right metric bundle for this ideal customer: age.over_65, income/six-figure households, disability rate, home ownership, median home value, and uninsured rate — collectively capturing demand, ability to pay, clinical need, aging-in-place intent, and payment friction. This is a strong, well-reasoned metric set. The only mismatch is the absence of any hospital/healthcare-facility proximity metric, which the brief specifically requested.

Overall (9): Coherent, well-structured, decision-oriented, and closes with a clear tiered recommendation. The hospital-proximity omission and a couple of minor county/CBSA data conflations keep it just short of a perfect score.
